items.title: Vercel Sandbox snapshots get up to 10x faster — pause/resume an agent session in under half a second
items.summary: Median snapshot creation drops from 4.4s to under 0.4s, and restore time falls from 500ms to 250ms at p50, by reusing frames in Vercel's own snapshot format (VHS) instead of writing fresh each time. Persistent sandboxes now snapshot automatically on stop and resume from the latest one — nothing to configure.
items.why: If you run coding agents in ephemeral sandboxes, pausing and resuming one now costs almost nothing instead of several seconds every time.
items.action: Spin up a persistent Vercel Sandbox, stop and resume it a few times, and compare the pause/resume latency against whatever sandbox or VM approach you use today.

eval.reason: Genuine quantified performance change (snapshot create and restore times), not pricing/benchmark PR. Checked against the Drive run log's Nov 5-10 history; not a duplicate.

items.title: OpenAI's Codex CLI 0.167 ships an agent command center for juggling multiple running agents
items.summary: `codex agents --no-daemon` opens a terminal view listing every agent session grouped by status and sorted by recency, with unread markers for finished work and pending approvals prioritized in the picker — works for embedded and remote App Server sessions too.
items.why: The single biggest pain of running several coding agents at once is losing track of which one actually finished — this puts that in one screen instead of five terminal tabs.
items.action: Update to Codex CLI 0.167+ and run `codex agents --no-daemon` next time you've got more than one task running, instead of switching between terminal tabs to check progress.

items.title: Simon Willison: Gemini 4 Carbon is open to everyone now — and his one-line prompt fix for agentic demos still holds
items.summary: Carbon (previously gated to "a subset of cyber defenders") is available to everyone as of this week, at $2/M input and $10/M output, doubling to $4/$20 on December 1st. Testing it in Google Antigravity with a three.js animation prompt, Willison had to explicitly add "build that into a standalone HTML file" to get a version with no external dependencies — without that line, the agent's output didn't run standalone.
items.why: A one-sentence addition to your prompt is the difference between an agent handing you a working, shareable file and one that only runs inside its own dev environment.
items.action: Next time you ask a coding agent for a quick demo or prototype, explicitly ask for "a standalone file with no external dependencies" rather than assuming it'll bundle things sensibly on its own.

items.title: Workday cut agent prototype time from 5 months to under a day by building on LangGraph and LangSmith
items.summary: Workday's internal developer platform — a durable agent server, data-access controls tied to its audit policies, a shared eval platform, and a Python SDK wrapping it all — took prototypes from a 4-to-5-month slog with no guarantee of reaching production down to a staging deployment in under a day. The team grew from 4 to roughly 30 people to build it. Beyond those two figures, the piece is light on hard numbers — no user counts, request volume, or cost data given.
items.why: A 5-months-to-a-day prototype number is the kind of concrete, checkable claim that's rare in vendor case studies — worth reading even with the honest caveat that it's the only hard metric in the piece.
items.action: If you're weighing whether a governance/eval layer (their "Agent System of Record") is worth building before scaling agent usage internally, this is a real reference architecture to compare against, not just a thought experiment.

items.title: How One Founder Manages 20 AI Coding Agents at Once — Ryan Carson, Untangle
items.summary: One "engineering manager" agent, mostly talked to by voice, runs up to 20 builder agents through a ticket board: a 15-minute automated check-in on every builder, capped review loops so QA agents can't argue forever, and a merge-queue manager. The one step Ryan won't skip: watching the video of each feature before it ships. Untangle now hires by having candidates record themselves shipping a real feature with an agent, has an agent rank the recordings, and runs a paid trial with the top five.
items.why: It's a concrete org-chart pattern for scaling past "one person babysitting a handful of chats" — with the specific guardrails (check-in interval, capped loops, a video-review gate) that make 20 agents tractable instead of chaos.

eval.reason: Concrete operational pattern for managing many coding agents, published Nov 9 on the AI Engineer channel; not a duplicate of anything in the Drive log history.

items.title: Your Agent Doesn't Need an LLM for Every Decision — Raymond Weitekamp, OpenProse
items.summary: Recursive language models are a well-known harness pattern for coding agents; Weitekamp applies the same recursive idea to fast classifiers ("System One" decision models) instead of full LLM calls, to build cheaper, faster workflows for coding agents, information retrieval and computer use. Published hours before this brief went out, so it's too fresh to have a comment section yet — judged on the talk's own description and chapter structure rather than audience reaction.
items.why: If every step of your agent pipeline reaches for a full LLM call, this is a concrete pattern for swapping the cheap, high-volume decisions out for a fast classifier instead — without giving up the recursive-harness structure you already like.
